src/hooks/usePushMessageHandler.ts.whatsWrong: The background/quit message handler calls `await NotificationService.scheduleLocalNotification(...)` with no try/catch. That method is not safe — on failure it executes `throw new Error('Failed to schedule notification')` (NotificationService.ts:395). scheduleNotificationAsync fails whenever POST_NOTIFICATIONS is denied (Android 13+), the notification permission is revoked, or the Expo notification channel isn't provisioned. When it throws, the exception propagates out of the async handler: `NotificationService.updateBadgeCount()` on line 104 never runs, and the promise returned to setBackgroundMessageHandler rejects inside the RN-Firebase headless JS task, producing a 'possibly unhandled promise rejection' / failed-task log.
src/hooks/usePushMessageHandler.ts.rootCause: Assuming scheduleLocalNotification cannot fail; it rethrows on any scheduling error.
src/hooks/usePushMessageHandler.ts.failureScenario: Android 13 device, user tapped 'Don't allow' on the notification permission prompt. A data-only push (no `notification` payload) arrives while the app is backgrounded/killed. Line 95 throws -> badge count is never updated for that push, and the headless task errors out instead of completing cleanly.
src/hooks/usePushMessageHandler.ts.fix: Wrap the schedule call: `if (title || body) { try { await NotificationService.scheduleLocalNotification(title || 'New Notification', body || 'You have a new update', remoteMessage.data); } catch (e) { console.warn('bg notif failed', e); } }` so the throw can never skip the badge update on line 104 or reject the headless task.

src/hooks/usePushMessageHandler.ts.whatsWrong: `getInitialNotificationFn!(msg).then(...)` is a floating promise with no `.catch()`. If the native getInitialNotification call rejects (native module error, some OEM ROMs, or transient Firebase init failure at cold start), it becomes an unhandled promise rejection. Unlike the other handlers this one has no error boundary at all.
src/hooks/usePushMessageHandler.ts.rootCause: Missing rejection handler on a native async call.
src/hooks/usePushMessageHandler.ts.failureScenario: Cold start on a Firebase-init edge case where getInitialNotification() rejects -> unhandled rejection surfaced at startup (dev red-box warning; in prod a logged unhandled rejection). No functional recovery path.
src/hooks/usePushMessageHandler.ts.fix: Append `.catch(() => {});` (or `.catch((e) => console.warn('getInitialNotification failed', e))`) to the promise chain ending at line 123.

src/hooks/useStoreProfile.ts.whatsWrong: fetchProfile awaits getStoreProfile(tenantId) then unconditionally calls setStoreProfile/setError/setLoading with no guard against tenantId changing mid-flight, the component unmounting, or refresh() being double-tapped. Responses can resolve out of order and there is no cancellation.
src/hooks/useStoreProfile.ts.rootCause: No request-id / mounted guard between the await (line 29) and the setState calls (lines 30, 33, 35). The service caches per-tenant, so an old tenant's request can resolve from cache faster (or a new tenant's network request slower) than the ordering they were dispatched in.
src/hooks/useStoreProfile.ts.failureScenario: Admin switches active tenant T1 -> T2 (TenantContext updates tenantId), so the effect re-runs and a second getStoreProfile fires. T1's in-flight request resolves AFTER T2's, so setStoreProfile(T1profile) runs last and the UI shows T1's store name/logo/phone/address while the app is scoped to T2 — a cross-tenant data leak violating the golden rule that tenantId scopes all state. Same overwrite happens on a fast refresh() double-tap. If the screen unmounts mid-fetch, the setState calls run on an unmounted component.
src/hooks/useStoreProfile.ts.fix: Add a request-id ref and only commit results from the latest request. import { ..., useRef } from 'react'; const requestIdRef = useRef(0); const fetchProfile = useCallback(async () => { if (!tenantId) { requestIdRef.current++; setStoreProfile(null); setLoading(false); return; } const requestId = ++requestIdRef.current; try { setLoading(true); setError(null); const profile = await storeProfileService.getStoreProfile(tenantId); if (requestId === requestIdRef.current) setStoreProfile(profile); } catch (err) { if (requestId === requestIdRef.current) { console.error('Error in useStoreProfile:', err); setError(err instanceof Error ? err : new Error('Failed to load store profile')); } } finally { if (requestId === requestIdRef.current) setLoading(false); } }, [tenantId]);

src/hooks/useStoreProfile.ts.whatsWrong: When tenantId is falsy the hook returns early after only setLoading(false); it never clears storeProfile, so a previously loaded tenant's profile persists.
src/hooks/useStoreProfile.ts.rootCause: Early-return branch omits setStoreProfile(null) (and setError(null)), so state from the prior tenantId leaks across a tenant change or logout.
src/hooks/useStoreProfile.ts.failureScenario: Admin is on tenant T1 with the profile loaded; they log out (or TenantContext clears), setting tenantId to undefined. fetchProfile hits the early return, leaving storeProfile holding T1's store name, logo, phone and address. Any consumer that renders storeProfile without also gating on tenantId shows the previous tenant's store to a logged-out/next context — violates GOLDEN_RULES 'clear all tenant state on tenant change'.
src/hooks/useStoreProfile.ts.fix: In the early-return branch clear the data: if (!tenantId) { setStoreProfile(null); setError(null); setLoading(false); return; } (folded into the finding-1 fix above).

src/hooks/useUserRegion.ts.whatsWrong: `parsed.code` is accepted and returned as CountryCode via a raw `as` cast with no check that it is an actual key of the phoneUtils `countries` map. The `parsed?.code` guard only rejects null/empty/undefined — ANY non-empty string (lowercase 'iq', a code that existed in an older build's picker but was later removed/renamed, or corrupted AsyncStorage) passes straight through. The JSDoc on line 8-9 promises the hook 'returns its code as a valid CountryCode', but the implementation guarantees no such validity.
src/hooks/useUserRegion.ts.rootCause: `setRegion(parsed.code as CountryCode)` trusts an arbitrary persisted string and bypasses validation via the `as` cast; the hook never checks membership in the supported-country set.
src/hooks/useUserRegion.ts.failureScenario: A user completed onboarding on an older/other build (or storage schema drifts, or the code was persisted lowercase) so user_region = {"code":"iq"} (or any code absent from the map). On SignInScreen, selectedCountry is seeded from this hook (line 304); at submit, getCountryInfo(selectedCountry) returns undefined (map miss, its declared non-optional return type lies), and `countryInfo.dialCode.replace(...)` on SignInScreen line 393 throws 'TypeError: undefined is not an object', crashing sign-in. PhoneLoginScreen (lines 175-177 and 216-217) crashes identically with no fallback. Proof this is real, not hypothetical: the team already patched RegisterScreen:294 (`|| getCountryInfo('IQ')`) and ForgotPasswordScreen:313 (`?? getCountryInfo('IQ')`) with comments explicitly blaming 'useUserRegion casts AsyncStorage JSON via `as CountryCode`' — but SignIn and PhoneLogin were left unguarded.

src/services/NotificationService.ts.whatsWrong: The INNER catch in getUserNotifications overwrites cachedNotifications with [], stamps lastCacheTime, and calls saveCacheToStorage() on ANY query failure. This runs BEFORE the outer catch (264-268), so the outer catch's cache-preserving branch (`if (this.cachedNotifications.length > 0) return ...`) can never help — the cache is already destroyed and persisted to disk.
src/services/NotificationService.ts.rootCause: Treating a transient fetch error as 'the user has zero notifications' and persisting that empty result, instead of keeping last-known-good data.
src/services/NotificationService.ts.failureScenario: User on a slow/dropped Iraqi mobile connection foregrounds the app. handleAppStateChange(502) or the realtime subscription (286) calls getUserNotifications(true). The Supabase call times out/throws -> the list is wiped to [], the notification screen goes blank, the unread badge drops to 0, and the empty array is written to AsyncStorage so it survives an app restart even after network returns (until the next successful fetch).
src/services/NotificationService.ts.fix: Do not wipe on transient error. Replace the inner catch body with: `} catch (error) { console.warn('notifications fetch failed, keeping cache'); return this.cachedNotifications; }` — leave cachedNotifications/lastCacheTime and storage untouched so stale-but-valid data is shown.

src/services/NotificationService.ts.whatsWrong: markAsRead mutates the cached notification object in place (`this.cachedNotifications[cacheIndex].read = true`). The array reference and the object reference are unchanged. This is inconsistent with markAllAsRead (343) which correctly builds new objects via map, and it does not set readAt.
src/services/NotificationService.ts.rootCause: In-place mutation of shared state that React consumers hold by reference; React can't detect a change when neither the array nor the item identity changes.
src/services/NotificationService.ts.failureScenario: The notifications screen stored `this.cachedNotifications` in useState (via the subscribe callback at 287/292). User taps one notification -> markAsRead flips read in place. The screen keeps the same array/object reference, so React does not re-render and the row still shows as unread (dot/bold), while getUnreadCount()/badge DO update — a visibly inconsistent UI until an unrelated re-render or realtime refetch replaces the objects.
src/services/NotificationService.ts.fix: Use an immutable update mirroring markAllAsRead: `this.cachedNotifications = this.cachedNotifications.map(n => n.id === notificationId ? { ...n, read: true, readAt: new Date() } : n); this.saveCacheToStorage();`

src/services/NotificationService.ts.whatsWrong: expoPushToken and fcmToken are declared but NEVER assigned anywhere in the file. registerForPushNotifications sets up Android channels and requests permission but never calls getExpoPushTokenAsync/getToken and always returns null; setupNativeListeners wires onMessage/onNotificationOpenedApp but never fetches an FCM token. So the guard at 48 (`if (this.expoPushToken || this.fcmToken)`) is always false and savePushTokenToSupabase is effectively unreachable with a real token. getPushToken() (507) always returns null.
src/services/NotificationService.ts.rootCause: Token acquisition step was never implemented (or removed), leaving the persistence pipeline permanently disabled.
src/services/NotificationService.ts.failureScenario: A user logs in on a real device. The backend needs users.push_token / fcm_token to target that device, but no token is ever written to Supabase, so server-initiated push to specific users silently never arrives. The failure is invisible (no error, no log) because the guarded branch just never executes.
src/services/NotificationService.ts.fix: In registerForPushNotifications, after channel setup and `if (!Device.isDevice) return null;`, actually acquire and store the token, e.g. `const fcm = await firebaseMessaging.getToken(msg); this.fcmToken = fcm;` and/or `const t = (await Notifications.getExpoPushTokenAsync({ projectId })).data; this.expoPushToken = t;`, then `await this.savePushTokenToSupabase(this.expoPushToken || '', this.fcmToken); return this.expoPushToken;`. Otherwise remove the dead token machinery.

src/services/OrderService.ts.whatsWrong: In subscribeToOrderUpdates and subscribeToOrder, `channel` is assigned asynchronously inside supabase.auth.getSession().then(...), but the returned cleanup closure `() => { if (channel) supabase.removeChannel(channel) }` may run BEFORE that promise resolves. If the consuming screen unmounts (user navigates away fast, or app backgrounded) before getSession settles, cleanup runs with channel===undefined (no-op), then the .then() later creates and .subscribe()s a channel that nothing will ever remove.
src/services/OrderService.ts.rootCause: Async resource creation with a sync teardown that captures the resource by a variable that isn't set yet, and no cancellation flag.
src/services/OrderService.ts.failureScenario: On a 320dp low-RAM Android with slow network, user opens OrdersScreen and immediately taps back. getSession() is still pending, so the effect cleanup runs (channel is undefined). A moment later getSession resolves, opens a Postgres realtime channel and subscribes. It is now orphaned. Repeating this navigation leaks one realtime channel + one getUserOrders(true) refetch each time until the socket connection limit is hit and realtime silently dies app-wide.

src/services/OrderService.ts.whatsWrong: searchOrders does `order.orderNumber.toLowerCase()`, `order.items.some(...)`, `item.productName.toLowerCase()`, `item.partNumber.toLowerCase()` with no null-guards. `items` comes straight from the DB jsonb column and items are typed `partNumber: string` but that guarantee doesn't hold for legacy/garbage rows. Any single order with `items: null`, or one item missing partNumber/productName, throws TypeError. Because the whole `.filter` runs inside the try/catch (536-549) that returns `[]`, ONE bad order makes EVERY search silently return zero results. Same swallow-to-empty pattern in getMostOrderedProducts (591 `order.items.forEach`) and a NaN in getOrderStatistics (526 `sum + order.totalUSD`).
src/services/OrderService.ts.rootCause: Trusting DB jsonb shape to match the TS interface, plus a broad try/catch that converts a data-shape bug into a silent empty result.
src/services/OrderService.ts.failureScenario: A migrated/older order row has `items: null` (or an item created from a flow that omitted partNumber). User goes to Orders, types any search term. searchOrders throws on `order.items.some`, the catch returns []. The user sees 'no orders found' for every query even though they have 20 valid orders. Same order also blanks the 'most ordered products' widget.
src/services/OrderService.ts.fix:
Defensive access:
```ts
return allOrders.filter(order =>
  (order.orderNumber || '').toLowerCase().includes(searchLower) ||
  (order.items || []).some(item =>
    (item.productName || '').toLowerCase().includes(searchLower) ||
    (item.partNumber || '').toLowerCase().includes(searchLower)
  )
);
```
Use `(order.items || []).forEach` at line 591 and `sum + (order.totalUSD || 0)` at 526.

src/services/OrderService.ts.whatsWrong: fetchAndCacheUserOrders and getOrderById map timestamps with raw `new Date(doc.created_at)` / `new Date(doc.updated_at)`. `new Date(null)` returns the 1970 epoch (a valid-looking wrong date) and `new Date(undefined)`/garbage returns Invalid Date. These feed getOrderTimeline (471,500), getDeliveryEstimate (708-712) and all UI date formatting. Ironically the file defines `safeToDate` (lines 6-14) for exactly this but never calls it — it is dead code.
src/services/OrderService.ts.rootCause: Bypassing the existing safeToDate guard on server data that can be null.
src/services/OrderService.ts.failureScenario: An order row has `updated_at` null (created but never status-updated, or migrated data). updatedAt becomes `new Date(null)` = 1970-01-01. The order timeline and 'Estimated delivery' then display 1970 / a nonsensical date to the customer. With truly malformed input it becomes Invalid Date and any comparison (getOrdersByDateRange, getMostOrderedProducts lastOrderDate) silently yields NaN/false.
src/services/OrderService.ts.fix:
Use the helper and fall back sensibly:
```ts
createdAt: safeToDate(doc.created_at) ?? new Date(),
updatedAt: safeToDate(doc.updated_at) ?? safeToDate(doc.created_at) ?? new Date(),
```
Apply at both 249-250 and 293-294.

src/services/OrderService.ts.whatsWrong: createOrder has no in-flight/idempotency guard. The order number `ORD-${Date.now()}-${Math.floor(Math.random()*1000)}` is not a dedupe key. Two overlapping calls insert two distinct orders. Worse: line 157 `.insert(...).select().single()` — if RLS permits INSERT but blocks the SELECT-back, `.single()` returns an error that is thrown AFTER the row was actually inserted, so the UI shows 'Failed to create order' and the user retries → a real duplicate order.
src/services/OrderService.ts.rootCause: No idempotency at the service layer and a create path that can throw after a successful write.
src/services/OrderService.ts.failureScenario: User taps 'Place Order' on a slow connection. The insert commits server-side but the response is lost / select-back errors. The UI shows failure; the user taps again. Now there are two identical paid orders. Same outcome from a fast double-tap if the calling screen doesn't guard the button.

src/services/auth/legacyEmailAuth.ts.whatsWrong: The `supabase.from('users').upsert({...})` call is awaited but its `{ error }` result is discarded. In the OTP-verified-session registration path, this is the ONLY write that persists the profile row (id/name/full_name/email/language). If the upsert fails (RLS rejection, unique-constraint, or a transient network blip on the 320dp low-RAM Android + slow-network scenario), the failure is swallowed. Execution proceeds to `getCurrentUserFresh()` (L60); when the row was never written, that method hits PGRST116 'no rows' and returns null (authService.ts L336), so L61 `if (fresh)` is false and the function falls through to the hand-built success object on L62-65. Net result: registerWithEmail RESOLVES with a valid-looking User and the UI reports 'account created', but the server has no profile row.
src/services/auth/legacyEmailAuth.ts.rootCause: Awaiting a Supabase mutation without destructuring/checking its `error`, combined with a fallback path (L62-65) that masks the missing row by fabricating a User.
src/services/auth/legacyEmailAuth.ts.failureScenario: User verifies email via OTP, taps Register on a flaky connection. updateUser (L51) succeeds but the users upsert times out. Error is swallowed; the function returns the L62-65 stub User; app navigates to Home as 'logged in'. On next app reopen getCurrentUserFresh finds no row (PGRST116) → user is bounced to login / profile shows blank name, and no order can attach to a real profile. The account is effectively half-created with no error ever surfaced.
src/services/auth/legacyEmailAuth.ts.fix: Capture and throw the error so the caller can surface a retry: `const { error: profErr } = await supabase.from('users').upsert({ id: session.user.id, name, full_name: name, email: cleanEmail, language: 'en' }); if (profErr) throw profErr;`

src/services/auth/legacyEmailAuth.ts.whatsWrong: `loginWithEmail` (L22-28) and `sendPasswordResetEmail` (L30-33) pass `email` straight through to AuthService WITHOUT trimming, whereas `registerWithEmail` (L44 `email.trim()`) and `isEmailRegistered` (L15 `email.trim()`) both trim. So the stored email is always whitespace-clean, but the login lookup is not: `signInWithIdentifier` (authService.ts L99) does `identifier.includes('@')` and forwards the raw string to `supabase.auth.signInWithPassword({ email })`. A leading/trailing space (common from Android autofill / email-keyboard suggestions) makes the login email differ from the trimmed value that was stored at registration.
src/services/auth/legacyEmailAuth.ts.rootCause: Inconsistent input normalization: two of the four entry points trim, two do not.
src/services/auth/legacyEmailAuth.ts.failureScenario: User registers 'ali@shop.iq' (trimmed and stored clean). Later, autofill/keyboard inserts a trailing space and login is called with 'ali@shop.iq '. GoTrue validates/matches the raw email and returns an auth error, so the user gets 'incorrect password' despite correct credentials — and cannot recover via password reset either, because sendPasswordResetEmail forwards the same untrimmed string. The register path proves the app itself treats surrounding whitespace as significant, which is exactly why login/reset must strip it too.
src/services/auth/legacyEmailAuth.ts.fix: Trim on the way in to match register: L27 `return AuthService.signInWithIdentifier(email.trim(), password);` and L32 `await AuthService.resetPassword(email.trim());`

src/services/auth/otpService.ts.whatsWrong: `latestConfirmation.confirm(code)` is typed `Promise<UserCredential | null>` in @react-native-firebase/auth. On Android SMS auto-retrieval (instant/auto verification), Firebase signs the user in automatically and `confirm()` resolves to `null`. Line 127 then reads `userCredential.user.uid` on `null` → TypeError, app crash on the verify screen.
src/services/auth/otpService.ts.rootCause: Trusting a Firebase API return that is explicitly typed as possibly-null.
src/services/auth/otpService.ts.failureScenario: Iraqi Android user on a device with Google Play SMS auto-retrieval: taps Send, the OS auto-fills and Firebase auto-signs-in, then `confirm(code)` resolves to null → `Cannot read property 'user' of null` → crash instead of a completed login.

src/services/auth/otpService.ts.whatsWrong: verifyOTP has NO in-flight guard (unlike sendOTP which uses `isSendingOtp`), and `latestConfirmation` is never cleared after a successful `confirm()`. A double-tap on the Verify button (or navigating back and retrying) fires `latestConfirmation.confirm(code)` a second time on an already-consumed confirmation, which Firebase rejects with `auth/session-expired` / `auth/code-expired`. The user — who is actually already signed in from the first call — sees a scary 'session expired' error.
src/services/auth/otpService.ts.rootCause: Concurrent-entry service function guarding sends but not verifies, plus module-global state that is never reset.
src/services/auth/otpService.ts.failureScenario: User on a slow connection taps Verify twice; call #1 succeeds and logs them in, call #2 reuses the same consumed confirmation and throws 'Verification session expired', overwriting the success UI with an error for an authenticated user.

src/services/categoryStore.ts.whatsWrong: save() and remove() both do an async readMock() followed by an async writeMock() with no serialization, mutex, or in-flight guard. Two overlapping calls each read the SAME list snapshot, mutate their own copy, and write it back — last write wins, so one mutation is silently lost. AsyncStorage getItem/setItem are genuinely async and interleave.
src/services/categoryStore.ts.rootCause: Read-modify-write on shared AsyncStorage without a serialization primitive; no queue/lock and no UI-level in-flight guard.
src/services/categoryStore.ts.failureScenario: Admin on the Category manager taps 'Add' for category A, then quickly taps 'Add' for B (or double-taps Save) before A's writeMock resolves. Both save() calls run readMock() and receive a 9-item list. A pushes -> writes 10 items. B pushes onto its own stale 9-item snapshot -> writes 10 items, overwriting A's write. Category A is permanently lost from storage. Same hazard for save-while-remove: a delete can resurrect a just-saved edit, or a save can resurrect a just-deleted category.
src/services/categoryStore.ts.fix: Serialize all mutations through a single promise chain, e.g. add `let opQueue: Promise<any> = Promise.resolve();` and wrap the body of save/remove: `opQueue = opQueue.then(async () => { const list = await readMock(); /* ...mutate...*/ await writeMock(list); return result; }); return opQueue;` (with a .catch to keep the chain alive). This makes each read-modify-write atomic relative to the others. Additionally guard the calling screen's Save/Delete buttons with an isSubmitting flag.

src/services/chatService.ts.whatsWrong: subscribeToMessages (and the three sibling subscribers) re-run a full fetchMessages() on EVERY postgres_changes event with no request sequencing. Concurrent/rapid events fire overlapping fetches whose network responses can arrive out of order; the last-resolving response wins, so a stale snapshot can overwrite a fresher one.
src/services/chatService.ts.rootCause: The realtime handler triggers an unordered async fetch; results are applied in arrival order, not issue order.
src/services/chatService.ts.failureScenario: On a 320dp Android over flaky Iraqi mobile data, an admin pastes two lines that insert msg A then msg B ~50ms apart. fetch(A) and fetch(A+B) both fire; fetch(A+B) returns first, then fetch(A) returns and calls callback with the list MISSING B. Because no further realtime event fires, B stays absent from the customer's chat until they scroll/reopen — a message silently 'disappears'.

src/services/chatService.ts.whatsWrong: `unread[oppositeRole] += 1` assumes both `user` and `admin` keys exist. The fallback `{...(conversation.unread || {user:0,admin:0})}` only covers a fully-null object, NOT a partial jsonb like `{user:3}`. If the target key is missing, `undefined + 1 = NaN`, which JSON-serializes to `null` in the DB.
src/services/chatService.ts.rootCause: Spread of a partial jsonb column leaves the incremented key undefined; the guard only handles the whole-object-missing case.
src/services/chatService.ts.failureScenario: A migrated/legacy conversation row has `unread = {user: 3}` (no admin key). A customer sends a message → oppositeRole='admin' → `unread.admin = undefined + 1 = NaN` → stored as `null`. getAdminUnreadCount does `c.unread?.admin || 0` → `null || 0 = 0`, so the admin's unread badge never increments for that message (the notification is lost). The next message recovers to 1, masking the off-by-one.

src/services/locationService.ts.whatsWrong: startTracking (line 97) and stopTracking (line 124) call JSON.parse(sessionsJson) with NO try/catch around the method body, unlike init() and the background task which both guard it. A corrupt or partially-written 'active_tracking_sessions' value throws synchronously and rejects the whole method.
src/services/locationService.ts.rootCause: Inconsistent error handling: two of the four readers of this AsyncStorage key parse defensively, two do not.
src/services/locationService.ts.failureScenario: App is killed by Android mid-write (low-RAM 320dp device), leaving invalid JSON in AsyncStorage. Delivery driver reopens the app and taps 'Stop tracking'. JSON.parse throws at line 124 BEFORE line 134 (stopLocationUpdatesAsync) and line 138 (mark row inactive) run. The foreground service keeps running, the driver's live location keeps broadcasting to the customer, and there is no way to stop it from this code path — battery drains and privacy leaks. If the caller has no .catch, it is also an unhandled rejection.
src/services/locationService.ts.fix: Wrap the parse in a safe helper, e.g. `let sessions = []; try { sessions = sessionsJson ? JSON.parse(sessionsJson) : []; } catch { sessions = []; }` in both startTracking and stopTracking, matching the try/catch already used in init() and the background task.

src/services/locationService.ts.whatsWrong: Both startTracking and stopTracking do an async read-modify-write on the same 'active_tracking_sessions' key: getItem (await) -> mutate array -> setItem (await). Concurrent calls interleave and the last writer clobbers the other's change (lost update).
src/services/locationService.ts.rootCause: No serialization/locking around the shared-key read-modify-write; the in-memory activeTrackingIds Set is not used as the source of truth for persistence.
src/services/locationService.ts.failureScenario: A driver is assigned two orders and starts tracking A and B nearly simultaneously (double dispatch, or fast tapping). startTracking(A) reads [], startTracking(B) reads []; A pushes and writes [A]; B pushes and writes [B] — A's session is lost. The background task at line 21-38 then only upserts coords for B, so the customer of order A sees a frozen/never-updating live marker even though the driver believes both are tracked. The stop path has the mirror bug (concurrent stop A + start B can drop B).
src/services/locationService.ts.fix: Serialize these mutations. Simplest: chain them through a single in-flight promise (`this.sessionsMutex = this.sessionsMutex.then(() => doUpdate())`), or derive the persisted list from the already-maintained in-memory `activeTrackingIds` Set under a lock, instead of re-reading storage each time.

src/services/locationService.ts.whatsWrong: stopTracking stops the OS location updates (line 134) BEFORE marking the Supabase live_tracking row inactive (line 138), and the Supabase update has no try/catch and is not retried. If line 138 rejects (offline), the row stays active:true forever while coords stop flowing.
src/services/locationService.ts.rootCause: Cleanup ordering + no offline tolerance: local teardown succeeds but the remote 'active:false' flag is best-effort and unprotected.
src/services/locationService.ts.failureScenario: Driver finishes delivery in an area with no signal and taps 'Stop'. Lines 126-136 run (sessions cleared, updates stopped), then line 138 rejects because the network is down. The customer's app keeps rendering the last-known coordinates as a 'live' driver pin indefinitely, and the rejected promise propagates as an unhandled rejection if the caller didn't await/catch.
src/services/locationService.ts.fix: Wrap line 138 in its own try/catch so a failed remote update never breaks local teardown, and mark the row inactive BEFORE stopping updates (or queue a retry / mark inactive via the next foreground sync). At minimum: `try { await supabase.from('live_tracking').update({ active:false, updated_at: new Date().toISOString() }).eq('id', orderId); } catch(e) { console.warn('failed to mark tracking inactive', e); }`

src/services/locationService.ts.whatsWrong: In the background task, `const { locations } = data; const location = locations[0];` (lines 15-16) run OUTSIDE the try/catch, which only starts at line 19. If `data` is truthy but `locations` is undefined, `locations[0]` throws an unguarded TypeError inside the OS task callback.
src/services/locationService.ts.rootCause: The try/catch is scoped one line too late — it starts after the destructuring/index access instead of wrapping it.
src/services/locationService.ts.failureScenario: The OS delivers a background-location payload where `data` is present but `data.locations` is undefined/null (garbage or an edge event). Line 16 throws 'Cannot read property 0 of undefined' uncaught inside the TaskManager callback, which can crash/kill the background task and stop all live tracking silently.
src/services/locationService.ts.fix: Move the try to cover the destructuring and guard the array: `if (data) { try { const { locations } = data; const location = locations?.[0]; if (location) { ... } } catch (err) { console.error(...); } }`

src/services/locationService.ts.whatsWrong: updateLocation and deleteLocation both accept an `adminId` parameter but never use it — the queries filter only by `.eq('id', locationId)`. The ownership check (canAdminModifyLocation) exists but is not enforced here, so any admin can update/delete any store location by id unless Supabase RLS blocks it.
src/services/locationService.ts.rootCause: Ownership enforcement was clearly intended (adminId is threaded in and a canAdminModifyLocation helper exists) but was dropped from the query, leaving an IDOR risk that silently depends on RLS being configured.
src/services/locationService.ts.failureScenario: Admin from tenant A calls updateLocation(locationOwnedByTenantB, {...}, adminA). With RLS misconfigured or a service-role client, tenant B's store data is overwritten/deleted. This violates the CLAUDE.md multi-tenancy golden rule (tenant must be part of every query).
